title: Deprecate legacy parameter-encoding endpoints and migration PRD
creator: Priya Kapoor
description: Summary: This PRD defines requirements to deprecate the legacy parameter-encoding API surface (legacy binary/protobuf parameter encoders exposed at /v0/params/encode and related endpoints) in favor of the unified, JSON-first encoding contract used by the unified inference endpoints. Motivation: legacy encodings have produced client fragmentation, caused frequent SDK edge-cases, and introduced interoperability and auditing blindspots for tokenization and parameter injection. Goal: provide a clear, staged sunset with SDK tooling, server-side adapter options, telemetry gates, and a communications timeline so customers and partner SDKs can migrate with minimal disruption. Scope: - All legacy parameter-encoding endpoints (both HTTP and websocket transports) and any model aliases that depend on non-JSON parameter payloads. - SDK helper methods that defaulted to legacy encoders. - Console tooling and docs that reference the old encoders. Out of scope: - Model-level alias deprecations unrelated to parameter encoding, unless they are direct dependencies of the endpoints above. - Dedicated/private appliance upgrade mechanics (covered in separate Private upgrade PRDs).
acceptance_criteria:
1) Announcement and migration docs published: public deprecation announcement, detailed migration guide, SDK migration playbook, and sample scripts must be available in the docs site.
2) SDK support: official SDK releases (JS, Python, Go) include opt-in compatibility adapters and clear deprecation warnings in logs; adapter tests pass in CI.
3) Telemetry: pre-deprecation telemetry (30 days before shutdown) shows at least 95% of requests can be routed to JSON-encoded endpoints or adapter translations without errors.
4) Backwards compatibility: server-side adapter must support 99.9% of legacy payloads for the grace period with documented failure modes.
5) Customer readiness: top 30 customers using the legacy endpoints have migration plans or accepted extended support.
6) Operational playbooks: runbooks and rollback criteria must be reviewed and approved by SRE and Support.
7) Final cutover: feature-flagged shutdown followed by a staged removal with telemetry gates and the option to extend the grace window if critical regressions are detected.
rollout_plan:
Phase 0 (Announcement - Week 0): Publish the deprecation schedule, migration guide, and provide sample CLI/SDK scripts.
Phase 1 (Adapter release - Weeks 2-6): Ship server-side adapter that translates legacy encodings to unified JSON, and SDK adapters that warn at runtime. Provide a canary region with adapter routing.
Phase 2 (Shadowing - Weeks 6-12): Route a percentage of legacy traffic through the adapter in shadow mode; monitor translation error rates, latency P95, and customer error tickets.
Phase 3 (Opt-in removal - Weeks 12-20): Enable a soft-404 for unadapted calls with detailed client error payloads; offer one-click console re-enable for customers on support call.
Phase 4 (Grace shutdown - Month 6): Disable legacy endpoints for new tenants and disable write operations; maintain read-only logs for 30 days.
Phase 5 (Hard removal - Month 7+): Fully remove routing for legacy endpoints and update public API catalog.
Notes: each phase gated by telemetry and customer readiness checkpoints. Minimum grace period: 6 months from announcement.
migration_guidance:
Developer-facing guidance to include: 1) Why JSON-first: determinism for tokenization, easier auditing, and consistent validation. 2) Simple examples mapping legacy binary/protobuf payloads to new JSON fields, with code snippets for JS/Python/Go. 3) SDK tasks: replace encodeParam() with encodeParamsJSON(), or add call to compatibilityAdapter.encodeLegacy(body). 4) Server-side tips: if you manage Dedicated instances, enable the adapter in the control plane or deploy the compiled adapter docker provided in the repo. 5) Edge cases: binary blobs used for custom token streams must be base64-wrapped in a JSON envelope; warn customers about size changes and token accounting differences. 6) Migration CLI: ship a tool that scans historical logs and auto-generates a mapping report for the top 10 parameter shapes per customer.
Backstop: customers unable to migrate can request extended support and a temporary tenancy flag (up to 12 months) with an escalation path through Solutions Engineering.
telemetry_gates:
Preconditions to advance phases (monitored daily): - Translation error rate <= 0.5% over 48h window. - Latency P95 for adapted requests increases no more than +30ms vs baseline. - No growth in customer errors or support tickets >10% week-over-week attributable to the change. - At least 80% of actively used SDKs updated to include deprecation warnings. If any gate fails, pause rollout and open a cross-functional war room.
Quantitative goals for GA: 95%+ migrated or adapted traffic; overall token accounting variance within +/-2% for migrated workloads.
rollback_criteria:
If at any checkpoint serious regressions appear (e.g., translation error rate >2%, customer-impacting outages, or an inability of top customers to authenticate): - Re-enable legacy routing for affected regions/tenants within 2 business hours. - Revert the adapter release in the control plane and publish an incident advisory. - Convene an incident review within 48 hours and re-baseline the timeline.
Rollback steps are documented in the SRE runbook and require sign-off from PM, SRE lead, and Head of Support.
qa_steps:
1) Unit and integration tests for adapters covering 100+ historical payload variants.
2) End-to-end regression tests comparing outputs of legacy encoder + model vs adapter+JSON encoder for parity tests on 200 curated prompts.
3) Load test the adapter at 2x peak observed legacy traffic for latency and memory pressure.
4) Canary region smoke tests with synthetic customers and live telemetry dashboards.
5) Post-cutover verification: automated nightly sweep that validates customer-specific mapping reports and flags any regression.
